headline: Ram Island Rocks Giving Up Slot Bass at First Light, Fluke Thick in the Sand Seams
subhead: The boulder fields are still cool and the bass know it — but the albies haven't shown their hand yet.
body_markdown:
First light on Ram Island this week, and the peanut bunker were doing what they do over the boulder field on the north side — bunching tight, nervous, ticking the surface like rain that isn't falling. That's the tell. Where the bait balls up and won't spread out, there's something underneath holding it there. I poled the skiff along the drop where the granite goes from four feet to twelve in about thirty yards, and on three separate passes I watched a bass roll through the bait without breaking the surface clean. Quiet takes. That's how they feed over rock — no crash, just a push of water and the bait scatters.

Water's been running cooler on the eastern end of the Sound than you'd expect for mid-July — New London's reading in the high 60s while the water off Kings Point to the west is already pushing 71. That gradient matters more than people think. The cooler pocket sitting over Fishers Island Sound is keeping bait concentrated and bass a little more willing to feed through the warmer parts of the day than they'd be if this whole stretch had turned into a bathtub. I'm not complaining about it. A little cold water in July off Stonington is money in the bank for August.

The breakwater has been my most consistent stop. Fished the outside face on the last two hours of the incoming tide Tuesday night with a black Slug-Go, weightless, worked slow along the riprap where the current wraps the eastern tip. Two slot bass, one at 29 inches, one just shy of 26, both came on the pause — let the plastic sit dead in the seam and they ate it sinking. Eels have worked too if you want to soak one on a fish-finder rig off the rocks after dark, but I've had better luck staying mobile with the soft plastic than sitting on bait right now. The fish aren't stacked, they're moving through on the tide, and you want to be able to follow them down the wall.

Wamphassuc Point and Esker Point have both been giving up fish on the dropping tide, first two hours especially, when the current pulls bait off the flats and funnels it past the ledges. Light tackle guys throwing 3-inch Albie Snax in bone white or bunker colors have done well working the current seams off both points. Nothing huge — mostly 22 to 26 inches — but steady enough that if you're covering water on foot or by kayak, you'll find willing fish.

Fluke have been the bright spot in Little Narragansett Bay and the sand pockets around Ram Island's southern flank. Drifting the mud-to-sand transitions in 10 to 18 feet with 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet in pink shine has produced fish to 22 inches, with a decent number of keepers mixed into the shorts. The bite's best on the last hour of the ebb when the water's moving enough to keep the bucktail ticking bottom but not so hard you're dragging a brick. Black sea bass are riding shotgun on the same structure — anything with hard bottom and current, the rockpiles off Fishers Island's west end especially, and they've been thick enough that if you're not targeting fluke specifically, you'll fill out a limit of sea bass before lunch.

Tog are off the table right now with the season closed, but I'll say this quietly — I've been marking fish stacked tight on a few of the deeper boulder piles off the east side of Fishers Island, the kind of structure that always loads up before the August reopener. Worth remembering where they are when the calendar turns.

Now the honest part. No albies yet. I know the calendar says we should start watching, and I have been — glassing the rips off Watch Hill and the reef off the breakwater every morning for that first nervous bait and the boil that doesn't belong to a bass. Nothing. Water's still a touch cool for them out here, and until that gradient closes up and the whole Sound settles into the mid-to-high 60s consistently, I wouldn't burn gas looking hard. Historically for this stretch of coast, it's mid-to-late August before the first real showing, sometimes into September if the bait's slow to arrive. I'll be out there checking anyway, because that's the job, but I'm not going to tell you to go looking yet.

Moon's building toward first quarter, which means the tides are getting a little more push behind them day by day. That's good news for the boulder-field bite — more current means more bait getting worked loose off the rocks, and more reason for bass to hold tight to structure rather than roam. If I had one morning this week, I'd fish the last of the incoming at the breakwater at first light, then slide over to Ram Island for the last two hours of the ebb and work the sand seams for fluke. Bring both rods. The rocks and the sand are both paying right now, just not at the same hour.
